texts.precise: Count each race's constructor result entries (`constructorResults` records, linked to the race and its circuit) and total their points, ignoring missing points. Group by race id and circuit country. Among the races whose entry count is above the average entry count across all races, list every race whose entry count is at least the 10th-highest entry count, so races tied at the cutoff are all included. Show the race id, the circuit `country`, the total points, the entry count, and how far the entry count is above the average (unrounded). Sort from the largest difference to the smallest.
texts.precise_other: Count each race's constructor result entries (`constructorResults` records, linked to the race and its circuit) and total their points, ignoring missing points. Group by race id and circuit country. Among the races whose entry count is above the average entry count across all races, list exactly 10 rows, cutting arbitrarily if races tie at 10th place. Show the race id, the circuit `country`, the total points, the entry count, and how far the entry count is above the average (unrounded). Sort from the largest difference to the smallest.
texts.open: Which are the top 10 races by how far their number of constructor result entries exceeds the average number of entries per race? Look only at races above that average. For each one, give the race id, the circuit's country, the total constructor points scored in that race (ignoring missing points), the number of entries, and the difference from the average. List them from the biggest difference down.

Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (4) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 1; for each kept record, return (1) column (4) of step 1; order the result rows by column (4) of step 1 descending (missing last); keep only the first 10 rows.

texts.precise: Link each invoice line item to its product (by product id) and to that product's category (by production type code), dropping lines with no match. For each product type description, compute the average `product_quantity` and the average cost difference, where each line's cost difference is `derived_product_cost` minus `derived_total_cost` (ignore missing values). Then take the mean of those category averages and keep only the categories whose average cost difference is above that mean. Return one row with three values: the average of those categories' average quantity, the average of their average cost difference, and the average of how much their average cost difference exceeds the mean. Don't round anything.
texts.precise_other: Link each invoice line item to its product (by product id) and to that product's category (by production type code), dropping lines with no match. For each product type description, compute the average `product_quantity` and the average cost difference, where each line's cost difference is the absolute value of `derived_product_cost` minus `derived_total_cost` (ignore missing values). Then take the mean of those category averages and keep only the categories whose average cost difference is above that mean. Return one row with three values: the average of those categories' average quantity, the average of their average cost difference, and the average of how much their average cost difference exceeds the mean. Don't round anything.
texts.open: Link each invoice line item to its product (by product id) and to that product's category (by production type code), dropping lines with no match. For each product type description, compute the average `product_quantity` and the average difference between `derived_product_cost` and `derived_total_cost` per line (ignore missing values). Then keep only the categories whose average difference is above the mean of all the category averages. Return one row with three values: the average of those categories' average quantity, the average of their average difference, and the average of how much their average difference exceeds that mean. Don't round anything.

Here A is line product cost (`Invoice_Line_Items.derived_product_cost`); B is line total cost including VAT (`Invoice_Line_Items.derived_total_cost`).
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (3) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 2 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which column (3) of step 1 is greater than column (1) of step 2; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) column (3) of step 1; (4) A − B. Here A is column (3) of step 1; B is column (1) of step 2.
Step 4 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 3; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (2) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (2) the average of column (3) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the average of column (4) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).

texts.precise: For each media type (grouped by name, using only tracks that are linked to a media type), compute its byte rate as the average of each track's `Bytes` divided by that track's `Milliseconds` (tracks with no size ignored). Then take the simple average of these rates across all media types. Which media types have a rate above that overall average? For each, give the media type name, its rate, and how far it is above the overall average (rate minus average), without rounding.
texts.precise_other: For each media type (grouped by name, using only tracks that are linked to a media type), compute its byte rate as the media type's total `Bytes` divided by its total `Milliseconds`. Then take the simple average of these rates across all media types. Which media types have a rate above that overall average? For each, give the media type name, its rate, and how far it is above the overall average (rate minus average), without rounding.
texts.open: Which media types (by name, counting only tracks that have a media type) have a bytes-per-millisecond rate higher than the simple average of that rate across all media types? For each, show the media type name, its rate, and how much it exceeds that average, unrounded.
texts.explicit:
Step 1. Start from each `Track` record; combine it with each `MediaType` record for which Media Type Id (`MediaType.MediaTypeId`) equals Media Type Id (`Track.MediaTypeId`), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); group the kept records by media type name (`MediaType.Name`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) media type name (`MediaType.Name`); (2) the average of A ÷ B in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none). Here A is track file size (`Track.Bytes`); B is track length (`Track.Milliseconds`).
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (2) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 2 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which column (2) of step 1 is greater than column (1) of step 2; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) A − B. Here A is column (2) of step 1; B is column (1) of step 2.
Conventions (SQLite's semantics): a condition that involves a missing value is undetermined, and neither it nor its negation holds. A formula is missing when any value in it is missing. Numbers are 64-bit integers or IEEE double-precision reals: ÷ is real-valued division (floating point); a division by 0 is missing; +, − and × of whole numbers stay whole unless the result leaves the 64-bit range, when it becomes a real; a sum of whole numbers that leaves that range is an error. a mod b is the remainder after both are truncated to whole numbers (missing when b truncates to 0). round rounds the double-precision value, halves away from zero; trunc truncates toward zero; text of a whole number is its decimal digits; sqrt, log10 and ln of a value outside their domain are missing; first_present is the first of its values that is not missing; nullif(a, b) is a, or missing when a equals b; larger and smaller are missing when any of their values is missing. Text is compared character by character, upper and lower case distinct (except in pattern matching). A date part of a value that is not a date is missing. When grouping or removing duplicates, missing values count as equal to each other.

texts.precise: For each invoice, together with its customer's country, compute the average `UnitPrice` of its invoice lines. Take the overall average of these invoice averages, and for each invoice compute its deviation (invoice average minus overall average). Then, for each country, average these deviations over its invoices. For each invoice, show the invoice id, country, average unit price, deviation from the overall average, and that deviation minus its country's average deviation. Sort by this last value from highest to lowest (blanks last) and return the top 10, including every invoice tied with the 10th one. Don't round.
texts.precise_other: For each invoice, together with its customer's country, compute the average `UnitPrice` of its invoice lines. Take the overall average of these invoice averages, and for each invoice compute its deviation (invoice average minus overall average). Then, for each country, average these deviations over its invoices. For each invoice, show the invoice id, country, average unit price, deviation from the overall average, and that deviation minus its country's average deviation. Sort by this last value from highest to lowest (blanks last) and return exactly 10 rows, breaking any tie at the cutoff arbitrarily. Don't round.
texts.open: Work out each invoice's average line `UnitPrice` (with its customer's country) and how far that is from the average across all invoices. Which are the top 10 invoices whose deviation sits furthest above their country's average deviation? Show the invoice id, country, average unit price, deviation from the overall average, and the deviation minus the country's average deviation, sorted highest first (blanks last) and unrounded.
texts.explicit:
Step 1. Start from each `InvoiceLine` record; combine it with each `Invoice` record for which Invoice Id (`Invoice.InvoiceId`) equals Invoice Id (`InvoiceLine.InvoiceId`), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); combine it with each `Customer` record for which Customer Id (`Customer.CustomerId`) equals Customer Id (`Invoice.CustomerId`), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); group the kept records by Invoice Id (`InvoiceLine.InvoiceId`) and customer country (`Customer.Country`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) Invoice Id (`InvoiceLine.InvoiceId`); (2) customer country (`Customer.Country`); (3) the average of price per unit of track sold (`InvoiceLine.UnitPrice`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (3) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 2 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) column (3) of step 1; (4) A − B. Here A is column (3) of step 1; B is column (1) of step 2.
Step 4. Start from the rows of step 3; group the kept records by column (2) of step 3; each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) column (2) of step 3; (2) the average of column (4) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 5. Start from the rows of step 3; combine it with the rows of step 4 for which column (2) of step 3 equals column (1) of step 4 (compared as text, character by character), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 3; (2) column (2) of step 3; (3) column (3) of step 3; (4) column (4) of step 3; (5) A − B; (6) the rank of the row among the result rows by A − B descending (missing last) (tied rows share a rank; the next rank skips). Here A is column (4) of step 3; B is column (2) of step 4.
Step 6 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 5; keep only the records for which column (6) of step 5 is at most 10; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 5; (2) column (2) of step 5; (3) column (3) of step 5; (4) column (4) of step 5; (5) column (5) of step 5; order the result rows by column (5) of step 5 descending (missing last).

texts.precise: Joining each transaction to its account (dropping transactions with no matching account), compute for each account statement frequency (`account.frequency`) the average signed transaction amount — `trans.amount` taken as positive when `trans.type` is 'PRIJEM', negative when it is 'VYDAJ', and left out (no value) for every other type, including 'VYBER' — and the average `trans.balance` over all its transactions. Then take the plain mean of those per-frequency average signed amounts, keep only the frequencies whose average signed amount is above that mean, and return a single row with: the average of their average signed amounts, the average of their average balances, and the average of how far their average signed amount exceeds the mean. Don't round.
texts.precise_other: Joining each transaction to its account (dropping transactions with no matching account), compute for each account statement frequency (`account.frequency`) the average signed transaction amount — `trans.amount` taken as positive when `trans.type` is 'PRIJEM', negative when it is 'VYDAJ' or 'VYBER' (treating 'VYBER' as a debit), and left out (no value) for every other type — and the average `trans.balance` over all its transactions. Then take the plain mean of those per-frequency average signed amounts, keep only the frequencies whose average signed amount is above that mean, and return a single row with: the average of their average signed amounts, the average of their average balances, and the average of how far their average signed amount exceeds the mean. Don't round.
texts.open: Linking each transaction to its account (skipping transactions without one), for each account statement frequency work out the average signed transaction amount — credits ('PRIJEM') positive, withdrawals negative, and any transaction that is neither left out — along with the average balance after the transaction. Then take the simple mean of those per-frequency signed averages, keep the frequencies above it, and give me one row: the average of their signed averages, the average of their balance averages, and the average amount by which their signed average exceeds the mean. Don't round.
texts.explicit:
Step 1. Start from each `trans` record; combine it with each `account` record for which the id of the account (`account.account_id`) equals Account number (`trans.account_id`), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); group the kept records by account statement issuance frequency (`account.frequency`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) account statement issuance frequency (`account.frequency`); (2) the average of the value of the first rule that applies: if transaction direction (credit/debit) (`trans.type`) is one of 'PRIJEM' (compared as text, character by character) (true when it equals one of them; undetermined when it is missing, or when it equals none of them and one of them is missing; otherwise false) then transaction amount (`trans.amount`); if transaction direction (credit/debit) (`trans.type`) is one of 'VYDAJ' (compared as text, character by character) (true when it equals one of them; undetermined when it is missing, or when it equals none of them and one of them is missing; otherwise false) then 0 − A; otherwise missing in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the average of account balance after transaction (`trans.balance`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none). Here A is transaction amount (`trans.amount`).
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (2) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 2 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which column (2) of step 1 is greater than column (1) of step 2; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) column (3) of step 1; (4) A − B. Here A is column (2) of step 1; B is column (1) of step 2.
Step 4 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 3; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (2) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (2) the average of column (3) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the average of column (4) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).

The relative ratio is the invoice's cost ratio divided by the average of all invoices' cost ratios (ignoring missing values). Return rows only when that overall average exists. Sort by the relative ratio from highest to lowest, with missing values last, show the top 10, and don't round anything.

The relative ratio is the invoice's cost ratio divided by the average of all invoices' cost ratios (ignoring missing values). Return rows only when that overall average exists. Sort by the relative ratio from highest to lowest, with missing values last, show the top 10, and don't round anything.
texts.open: For each invoice in `Invoice_Line_Items`, show the invoice number, the invoice's ratio of product cost (`derived_product_cost`) to total cost (`derived_total_cost`), how many line items it has, and that ratio divided by the average ratio across all invoices. Ignore missing values throughout, and return rows only when that overall average exists. Sort by the relative figure from highest to lowest, with missing values last, show the top 10, and don't round anything.

texts.precise: Matching examinations to their patients, count the distinct examined patients (`Examination.ID`) for each `SEX` value (blank and missing sexes are their own groups) and work out each sex's share of the combined count. Among the sexes whose count is above the average count per sex, give one row with the total of their counts, the average of their shares, and the average amount by which their counts exceed that per-sex average.
texts.precise_other: Matching examinations to their patients, count the examination records for each `SEX` value (blank and missing sexes are their own groups) and work out each sex's share of the combined count. Among the sexes whose count is above the average count per sex, give one row with the total of their counts, the average of their shares, and the average amount by which their counts exceed that per-sex average.
texts.open: Looking at the examination data by patient sex (blank and missing sexes as their own groups), how many were examined in each sex, and what share of the overall total is that? For the sexes above the per-sex average, give one row with their combined total, their average share, and on average how far above the per-sex average they are.
texts.explicit:
Step 1. Start from each `Examination` record; combine it with each `Patient` record for which identification of the patient (`Patient.ID`) equals identification of the patient (`Examination.ID`), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); group the kept records by patient sex (`Patient.SEX`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) patient sex (`Patient.SEX`); (2) the number of distinct non-missing values of identification of the patient (`Examination.ID`) in the group.
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the sum of column (2) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 2 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) A ÷ B. Here A is column (2) of step 1; B is column (1) of step 2.
Step 4. Start from the rows of step 3; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (2) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 5. Start from the rows of step 3; combine it with the rows of step 4 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 4 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which column (2) of step 3 is greater than column (1) of step 4; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 3; (2) column (2) of step 3; (3) column (3) of step 3; (4) A − B. Here A is column (2) of step 3; B is column (1) of step 4.
Step 6 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 5; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the sum of column (2) of step 5 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (2) the average of column (3) of step 5 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the average of column (4) of step 5 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).

For each trader type, return the trader type, the average record count of the kept pairs, their average share, and the average amount by which their share exceeds the trader type's average share, without rounding.
texts.open: Link the `advancedbehavior` records to their transaction via `translink` and on to the trader who made it (skip anything that doesn't match), and count records for each transaction (`translink`) and trader type combination. Each combination's share is its count over the total for its trader type. Looking only at combinations whose share sits on the upper side of the average share for their trader type, give me, per trader type, the average count, the average share, and the average margin over the trader type's average share — no rounding.

Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; group the kept records by column (2) of step 1; each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) column (2) of step 1; (2) the sum of column (3) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which column (2) of step 1 equals column (1) of step 2 (compared as text, character by character), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) column (3) of step 1; (4) A ÷ B. Here A is column (3) of step 1; B is column (2) of step 2.
Step 4. Start from the rows of step 3; group the kept records by column (2) of step 3; each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) column (2) of step 3; (2) the average of column (4) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 5. Start from the rows of step 3; combine it with the rows of step 4 for which column (2) of step 3 equals column (1) of step 4 (compared as text, character by character), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which column (4) of step 3 is greater than column (2) of step 4; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 3; (2) column (2) of step 3; (3) column (3) of step 3; (4) column (4) of step 3; (5) A − B. For each one, show the telescope reference, its average modulation index, how far it is above the overall average (its average minus the overall average), and its average divided by the overall average. Sort by that ratio from highest to lowest and return the top 10, without rounding.
texts.open: For each telescope (`telescref`) in the signals table, compute its average modulation index (`modindex`), ignoring missing values. Then list the telescopes whose average is above the overall average, taking the overall average as the mean of the per-telescope averages. For each one, show the telescope reference, its average modulation index, how much it exceeds the overall average, and its average as a ratio to the group average. Return the top 10 by that ratio, highest first, without rounding.

texts.precise: For each funding source (`projects.fundflux`), using the spatial records (`scanspatial`) whose `arcref` matches a project's `arcregistry` and dropping any that don't match, work out two numbers. The first is the average over the records of (`boxy` − `boxx`) ÷ `boxx`. The second is the area-to-volume ratio, taken as the records' total `aream2` divided by their total `volm3`. Ignore missing values. Then take the simple average of that area-to-volume figure across all funding sources. List only the funding sources whose figure is above that average. Show the funding source, the average Y-vs-X difference, the area-to-volume figure, and how far the figure is above the cross-source average, with no rounding.

The first is the average over the records of (`boxy` − `boxx`) ÷ `boxx`. The second is the average over the records of each record's area-to-volume ratio (`aream2` ÷ `volm3`). Ignore missing values. Then take the simple average of that area-to-volume figure across all funding sources. List only the funding sources whose figure is above that average. Show the funding source, the average Y-vs-X difference, the area-to-volume figure, and how far the figure is above the cross-source average, with no rounding.
texts.open: Using the spatial records (`scanspatial`) whose `arcref` matches a project's `arcregistry` and dropping any that don't match, look at each funding source (`projects.fundflux`). For each one, give the average relative difference between `boxy` and `boxx`, computed per record as (`boxy` − `boxx`) ÷ `boxx`, and give its area-to-volume ratio (`aream2` to `volm3`). Ignore missing values. Which funding sources have a ratio above the simple average of that ratio across all funding sources? Show the funding source, the average Y-vs-X difference, the ratio, and how far the ratio is above that average, with no rounding.

Start from each `scanspatial` record; combine it with each `projects` record for which arcregistry (`projects.arcregistry`) equals Project ID linking spatial data (`scanspatial.arcref`) (compared as text, character by character), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); group the kept records by funding source (`projects.fundflux`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) funding source (`projects.fundflux`); (2) the average of (A − B) ÷ B in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) C ÷ D. Here A is bounding box Y length (`scanspatial.boxy`); B is bounding box X length (`scanspatial.boxx`); C is the sum of area (`scanspatial.aream2`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); D is the sum of volume (`scanspatial.volm3`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (3) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 2 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which column (3) of step 1 is greater than column (1) of step 2; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) column (3) of step 1; (4) A − B. Here A is column (3) of step 1; B is column (1) of step 2.

Second, the average bandwidth usage (`telescopes.bandusagepct`), averaging per station first and then across stations (missing values ignored). Third, how many there are with that phase. Fourth, what share of the overall total that is. Don't round.

Step 1. Start from each `telescopes` record; combine it with each `observatories` record for which observstation (`observatories.observstation`) equals observstation (`telescopes.observstation`) (compared as text, character by character), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); group the kept records by observstation (`telescopes.observstation`) and moon phase (`observatories.lunarstage`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) observstation (`telescopes.observstation`); (2) moon phase (`observatories.lunarstage`); (3) the average of bandwidth usage share (`telescopes.bandusagepct`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (4) the number of records in the group.
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; group the kept records by column (2) of step 1; each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) column (2) of step 1; (2) the average of column (3) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the sum of column (4) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 2; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the sum of column (3) of step 2 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 4 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 2; combine it with the rows of step 3 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 3 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 2; (2) column (2) of step 2; (3) column (3) of step 2; (4) A ÷ B. Here A is column (3) of step 2; B is column (1) of step 3.

texts.precise: Match each scan in `scans` to its site in `sites` on site code (`zoneref` = `zoneregistry`), leaving out scans whose site code isn't found. Group by the site's health and safety status (`healtheval`). For each status, compute the total of `scancount` and a GB-per-minute rate obtained by first dividing each scan's own `gbsize` by its own `spanmin` and then taking the mean of those per-scan ratios. Missing values are ignored in sums and averages. Compute the average of that rate across all statuses and keep only the statuses whose rate is strictly above it (none if that average is missing). List the status, the total scan count, the rate, and the rate minus that average. No rounding.
texts.precise_other: Match each scan in `scans` to its site in `sites` on site code (`zoneref` = `zoneregistry`), leaving out scans whose site code isn't found. Group by the site's health and safety status (`healtheval`). For each status, compute the total of `scancount` and a GB-per-minute rate obtained by adding up all the status's `gbsize` and dividing that by the sum of all its `spanmin` (a ratio of totals, not an average of per-scan ratios). Missing values are ignored in sums and averages. Compute the average of that rate across all statuses and keep only the statuses whose rate is strictly above it (none if that average is missing). List the status, the total scan count, the rate, and the rate minus that average. No rounding.
texts.open: For scans matched to their site (skip any whose site code isn't in `sites`), break things down by the site's health and safety status (`healtheval`). For each status, show the total number of scans (`scancount`) and the GB per minute of scanning, based on `gbsize` and `spanmin`, ignoring missing values. Only include statuses whose GB per minute is strictly above the average of that figure across statuses (none if that average is missing). Show the status, the total scans, the GB per minute, and how much it exceeds that average. No rounding.
texts.explicit:
Step 1. Start from each `scans` record; combine it with each `sites` record for which Primary key for a site (`sites.zoneregistry`) equals zoneref (`scans.zoneref`) (compared as text, character by character), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); group the kept records by health and safety approval status (`sites.healtheval`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) health and safety approval status (`sites.healtheval`); (2) the sum of scans in set (`scans.scancount`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the average of A ÷ B in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none). Here A is scan file size (`scans.gbsize`); B is scanning duration (`scans.spanmin`).
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (3) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 2 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which column (3) of step 1 is greater than column (1) of step 2; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) column (3) of step 1; (4) A − B. Here A is column (3) of step 1; B is column (1) of step 2.
Conventions (SQLite's semantics): a condition that involves a missing value is undetermined, and neither it nor its negation holds. A formula is missing when any value in it is missing. Numbers are 64-bit integers or IEEE double-precision reals: ÷ is real-valued division (floating point); a division by 0 is missing; +, − and × of whole numbers stay whole unless the result leaves the 64-bit range, when it becomes a real; a sum of whole numbers that leaves that range is an error. a mod b is the remainder after both are truncated to whole numbers (missing when b truncates to 0). round rounds the double-precision value, halves away from zero; trunc truncates toward zero; text of a whole number is its decimal digits; sqrt, log10 and ln of a value outside their domain are missing; first_present is the first of its values that is not missing; nullif(a, b) is a, or missing when a equals b; larger and smaller are missing when any of their values is missing. texts.precise: Group invoices by billing state (`Invoice.BillingState`), treating invoices with no billing state as one group of their own, and count the invoices in each group. Work out each group's share of the invoices (its count over the sum of all the groups' counts) and the average count per group. Keep the groups whose count is above that average. Return one row with: the total number of invoices in those groups, the average of their shares, and the average amount by which their count exceeds the average count (count minus average). Don't round.
texts.precise_other: Group invoices by billing state (`Invoice.BillingState`), leaving out invoices with no billing state entirely, and count the invoices in each group. Work out each group's share of the invoices (its count over the sum of all the groups' counts) and the average count per group. Keep the groups whose count is above that average. Return one row with: the total number of invoices in those groups, the average of their shares, and the average amount by which their count exceeds the average count (count minus average). Don't round.
texts.open: Count invoices by billing state, and work out each billing state's share of the invoices (its count over the sum of all the counts) and the average invoice count per billing state. Keep the billing states with more invoices than that average. Give one row with: the total number of invoices across them, their average share, and on average how many invoices above the average count they are (count minus average). No rounding.
texts.explicit:
Step 1. Start from each `Invoice` record; group the kept records by billing state or province (`Invoice.BillingState`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) billing state or province (`Invoice.BillingState`); (2) the number of records in the group.
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the sum of column (2) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 2 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) A ÷ B. Here A is column (2) of step 1; B is column (1) of step 2.
Step 4. Start from the rows of step 3; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (2) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 5. Start from the rows of step 3; combine it with the rows of step 4 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 4 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which column (2) of step 3 is greater than column (1) of step 4; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 3; (2) column (2) of step 3; (3) column (3) of step 3; (4) A − B. Here A is column (2) of step 3; B is column (1) of step 4.
Step 6 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 5; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the sum of column (2) of step 5 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (2) the average of column (3) of step 5 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the average of column (4) of step 5 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).

texts.precise: Linking lab records to patients by `ID` (dropping unmatched lab records), first average each patient's (`ID`, `SEX`) `ALB` and their per-test ratio of `UN` to `T-BIL`. Then, for each sex (leaving out patients whose `SEX` is blank or missing), average those patient-level figures. Which sexes have an average `ALB` above the mean of the sex-level `ALB` averages? Show the sex, its average `ALB`, its average `UN`/`T-BIL` ratio, and how far its `ALB` average is above that mean. Averages ignore missing values (including ratios that can't be computed); don't round.

Which sexes have an average `ALB` above the mean of the sex-level `ALB` averages? Show the sex, its average `ALB`, its average `UN`/`T-BIL` ratio, and how far its `ALB` average is above that mean. Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; group the kept records by column (2) of step 1; each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) column (2) of step 1; (2) the average of column (3) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the average of column (4) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 2; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (2) of step 2 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).

texts.precise: Treat each individual record in `scanfeatures` as one unit, without combining records from the same site; its count is that record's artifact count (`articount`), and missing counts are ignored in totals and averages. Each unit's share is its count divided by the overall artifact total across all of `scanfeatures`; if the overall total is missing, return no rows. The average share is the mean of the units' shares (ignoring missing shares); if that average is missing, return no rows. The average share is the mean of the units' shares (ignoring missing shares); if that average is missing, return no rows. For each unit show the site code, its artifact count, its share, and its share minus the average share. Sort by that difference from highest to lowest with missing values last, and keep the top 10.
texts.open: In the feature scan data, which 10 site artifact counts (`articount`, identified by site code `zoneref`) stand furthest above the average in their share of all artifacts? Each count's share is that count divided by the overall artifact total across all of `scanfeatures` (return nothing if the overall total is missing), and the average share is the mean of those shares (again return nothing if that average is missing). For each, give the site code, the artifact count, its share, and its share minus the average share. Ignore missing counts, and sort from the highest difference down with missing values last.

Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the sum of column (2) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 2 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) A ÷ B. Step 5 (the answer). Average the invoice ratios across all invoices, and keep only the invoices whose ratio is above that average. Average these patient figures within each sex (every `SEX` value, blank or missing included, as its own group). Keep the sexes whose average `APTT` − `PT` is above the mean of the sex-level `APTT` − `PT` averages. Give a single row averaging, across those sexes: the `ALB` − `TP` figure, the `APTT` − `PT` figure, and how far the `APTT` − `PT` figure exceeds that mean. Averages ignore missing values; don't round.

Average these patient figures within each sex (every `SEX` value, blank or missing included, as its own group). Keep the sexes whose average `APTT` − `PT` is above the mean of the sex-level `APTT` − `PT` averages. Give a single row averaging, across those sexes: the `ALB` − `TP` figure, the `APTT` − `PT` figure, and how far the `APTT` − `PT` figure exceeds that mean. Step 2. Step 5 (the answer). texts.precise: For each film rating, find the average film `length` (ignoring films with no length) and the per-day rental price, defined as the average over the rating's films of each film's `rental_rate` divided by its `rental_duration`. Then take the simple mean of those per-day prices across the ratings, with each rating counting once, and keep only the ratings whose per-day price is above that mean. For those ratings, give one row with the average of their average lengths, the average of their per-day prices, and the average amount by which their per-day price exceeds the cross-rating mean. Don't round anything.
texts.precise_other: For each film rating, find the average film `length` (ignoring films with no length) and the per-day rental price, defined as the rating's average `rental_rate` divided by its average `rental_duration`. Then take the simple mean of those per-day prices across the ratings, with each rating counting once, and keep only the ratings whose per-day price is above that mean. For those ratings, give one row with the average of their average lengths, the average of their per-day prices, and the average amount by which their per-day price exceeds the cross-rating mean. Don't round anything.
texts.open: For each film rating, look at its average film length (ignoring films with no length) and its rental rate per day of rental. Which ratings have a per-day rate above the simple mean of the ratings' per-day rates, with each rating counting once? For just those ratings, give one row with their average length, their average per-day rate, and the average amount by which they exceed that mean. Don't round anything.
texts.explicit:
Step 1. Start from each `film` record; group the kept records by film content rating (`film.rating`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) film content rating (`film.rating`); (2) the average of film running time (`film.length`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the average of A ÷ B in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none). Here A is rental price (`film.rental_rate`); B is allowed rental duration (`film.rental_duration`).
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (3) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 1; combine it with the rows of step 2 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 2 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which column (3) of step 1 is greater than column (1) of step 2; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 1; (2) column (2) of step 1; (3) column (3) of step 1; (4) A − B. Here A is column (3) of step 1; B is column (1) of step 2.
Step 4 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 3; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (2) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (2) the average of column (3) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the average of column (4) of step 3 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
